#5821. GLP-1s' Effects on Cancer Risk May Be Influenced by Diabetes Severity

— Retrospective cohort analyses show variable performance versus other diabetes drugs

Diabetic patients treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists had a lower cancer risk versus insulin and sulfonylureas but not other diabetes medications, although the benefits varied by diabetes severity, a large cohort analysis with multiple comparators showed.

Three years after starting treatment for type 2 diabetes, propensity-matched cohort analyses showed that patients treated with GLP-1 agonists had a 2.01% estimated risk of obesity-related cancers (ORCs) as compared with 3.26% for insulin users and 2.85% versus 3.98% for sulfonylurea users. At 5 years, risk differences still favored GLP-1 drugs over insulin and sulfonylureas in almost all diabetes-severity categories.

ORC risk with GLP-1 agonists did not differ significantly as compared with patients who started treatment with metformin, a sodium-glucose transport 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, or a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) inhibitor. Patients with moderate- and high-severity diabetes fared better with SGLT2 inhibitor treatment during the first 3 years.

The results suggest that a patient's baseline diabetes profile may influence the effects of treatment on cancer risk, reported Jesús Gibran Hernández-Pérez, PhD, of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, and colleagues in JAMA Network Open.

"For me, the main message is that when we talk about GLP-1 receptor agonists and cancer risk, we need to ask, 'compared with which medication, and in which patients,"' Hernández-Pérez told MedPage Today. "We observed lower obesity-related cancer incidence compared with insulin and sulfonylureas, particularly among adults with lower diabetes severity. However, we did not find consistent differences compared with metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, or SGLT2 inhibitors."

"These findings are broadly reassuring, but they do not establish that GLP-1 receptor agonists prevent cancer or that insulin or sulfonylureas cause cancer," he added. "These medications are often prescribed at different stages of diabetes and for different clinical reasons. That is really the point that we wanted to bring attention to, that some of the differences we observe may come from the patients' underlying health and treatment history, even after adjustment."

A patient's baseline profile matters when interpreting the data, and treatment decisions should still be guided by established metabolic, cardiovascular, and kidney benefits and individual patient needs.

"I would not recommend changing an otherwise appropriate treatment solely to reduce cancer risk based on our findings," said Hernández-Pérez.

The study adds context to data regarding cancer risk in patients with obesity and/or diabetes and use of GLP-1 receptor agonists. Both obesity and diabetes are associated with increased cancer risk. One recent study showed that GLP-1 agonist use was associated with a reduced risk for 12 of 13 ORCs included in the analysis. Another recent study showed a reduced risk of ORCs and mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity treated with GLP-1 drugs. Yet another study, limited to patients with type 2 diabetes, showed a reduced risk for 10 of 13 ORCs.

Hernández-Pérez and colleagues continued the line of research by conducting five separate active-comparator studies examining cancer risk in patients with type 2 diabetes treated with one of five types of diabetes medications compared with GLP-1 receptor agonists and stratified by baseline diabetes severity. Using PCORnet electronic health record data, they identified 359,595 adults with type 2 diabetes treated at a single center from January 2010 through July 2025.

Each study was re-emulated by type 2 diabetes severity, as determined by diabetes-associated complications documented prior to starting one of the drugs, including macrovascular disease and various stages of diabetic kidney disease and other cardiometabolic comorbidities. The design was intended to identify "contexts in which associations were most apparent, rather than proving treatment superiority for cancer outcomes." Outcomes were assessed after 3 and 5 years of follow-up.

For the 3-year follow-up versus insulin, GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with lower cancer risk across all of the disease-severity categories. Comparisons reached statistical significance only in the overall analysis (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.77) and in the low-severity patients (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.47-0.78). The same pattern emerged after 5 years of follow-up, with all hazards favoring GLP-1 agonists, achieving statistical significance in the overall and low-severity analyses.

Analyses for GLP-1 drugs versus sulfonylureas achieved statistical significance at 3 years in the overall analysis (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.54-0.84) and low disease-severity group (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.79). In patients with the most severe diabetes, treatment with a GLP-1 receptor agonist was associated with a higher estimated cancer risk, though the difference was not statistically significant (HR 1.49, 95% CI 0.74-2.99). The significant advantage for GLP-1 agonist users persisted at 5 years for overall risk of ORCs and risk in patients with low-severity diabetes. The risk difference favored GLP-1 drugs for moderately severe diabetes but did not achieve statistical significance and trended in favor of sulfonylureas for patients with the most severe diabetes.

In the 3-year comparison with metformin, patients treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists had lower hazards in the overall comparison and in patients with low- and moderate-severity diabetes (HR 0.82 to HR 0.73), but none of the differences reached statistical significance. The cancer hazard trended slightly higher with GLP-1 agonists in the high-severity comparison (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.58-1.96). The 5-year results showed lower hazards with GLP-1 drugs overall and in all disease-severity categories, but none of the differences achieved statistical significance (HR 0.91 to HR 0.85).

The 3-year comparison for GLP-1 receptor agonist and SGLT2 inhibitor use trended in favor of the former in the overall analysis and for patients with low-severity diabetes (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.52-1.25 and HR 0.77, 95% C 0.47-1.25), but favored SGLT2 inhibitor use for the moderate- and high-severity groups (HR 1.53, 95% CI 0.42-5.58 and HR 2.07, 95% CI 0.69-6.25). The 5-year results were similar except the GLP-1 drug advantages in the overall and low-severity comparisons were smaller and the HRs favoring SGLT2 inhibitor use were slightly larger in patients with moderate- and high-severity diabetes.

The 3-year comparison with DPP4 inhibitors showed non-significant trends favoring GLP-1 receptor agonist use overall (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65-1.09) and in patients with low-severity diabetes (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.59-1.07). In general, differences moved closer to 1.00 in the 5-year comparisons.

The results add to the existing evidence base, but numerous questions remain open, said Hernández-Pérez. As examples, he cited effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on specific cancer types, impact of sustained versus intermittent or inconsistent treatment, and head-to-head comparisons of GLP-1 agonists with respect to their effects on cancer risk.

#5820. What's The Worst Road Trip You've Ever Taken?

It might be getting colder outside, but road trips aren't over for the year yet. The busiest driving days are the days around Thanksgiving and Christmas, as people travel to visit loved ones. Some might be just heading across town. Others are driving around the state, while others are traveling across the country. And while the old adage that "it's not about the destination, it's about the journey" might be true, the journey can be crummy. What's the worst road trip you've ever taken?

Plenty of things can spoil a long drive. Snow is on the way in the next few months, and that's always something to look out for, but with hurricane season winding down, you can still get caught in a torrential downpour or an early winter storm with lots of non-frozen water. Never underestimate how dangerous precipitation can be out on the road. I learned that lesson the hard way while driving across Pennsylvania before the start of a fall semester in college. It was raining so hard that I couldn't see beyond my hood. The curtain of water made visibility so poor that I had to pull over beneath an underpass for shelter.

A big part of driving for hours at a time is staying comfortable behind the wheel. When it's scorching hot outside, a good climate control system is the only thing that can keep you cool inside a car because rolling down the windows will literally just blow hot air into your face. If an issue crops up with your car's air conditioning unit, it's never an easy fix. A road trip, especially a summer one, where your air conditioning breaks can be particularly brutal. You either have to suffer through oppressive temperatures, or stop somewhere unfamiliar to get a fix — potentially delaying your trip quite a bit.

A bad road trip could be well outside the bounds of one that's got expensive repairs or uncomfortable conditions. It could be an ultra-long trip that goes exclusively past boring, endless, flat terrain with no music to keep you entertained.

You tell us what your idea of a bad road trip is by leaving the story of your worst road trip in the comment section below. Include all the aggravating details along with the pertinent information, like when and where you were driving.

#5818. Here Are All The Cool Cars Elon Musk Could Have Bought Instead Of Spending $474,000,000 On Political Ads

The midterm elections are over. If you live in a swing state like I do, you've probably been inundated with political attack ads, texts, and phone calls for the last several months. This has been the most expensive election in U.S. history, and much of the blame for that can be laid on the shoulders of the richest man in the world, and one-time Jalopnik contributor, Elon Musk. After Joe Biden spurned him in 2021, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has become the single largest political donor in history, spending hundreds of millions of dollars in support of Republican political campaigns. According to recent reports Musk spent an incredible 474 million American greenbacks nationwide, with some $200 million of that spent supporting Ken Paxton's campaign for U.S. Senate in his adopted home state of Texas.

Megadonor Musk's efforts were all in vain as every one of the political campaigns he supported in swing states failed. With economic inequality, an incredibly unpopular war, and AI data centers among the top concerns for American voters in this election, it certainly feels like these results are a referendum on Musk himself. Musk spent the weeks leading up to the election using his social media platform Twitter to call Texas Senator Elect James Talarico a "far left extremist" when he wasn't using it to promote his AI chatbot or retweet the thoughts of vile bigots.

So, after all that, it seems the world's only trillionaire decided to throw away half a billion dollars on unelectable candidates and an extremely unpopular agenda. $474 million is a small fraction of Elon's net worth, just under half a tenth of a percent, in fact. He probably won't even notice the money is gone, but the fact remains that he could have spent that money instead on something much cooler. He could have bought 6,423 brand new base model Corvettes, for example. He could have given each of the 500 people living in SpaceX company town Starbase, Texas, 12 Corvettes as a gift.

What if he had grander ambitions than Corvettes? Let's look into it.

Back in August, if Musk had found himself at Monterey Car Week instead of pumping money into his super pacs, he could have really cleaned house and built himself a really cool collection of some of the most important cars in history. As the CEO of the world's most valuable car company, Musk must have at least some interest in cars, right? He did own a McLaren F1 at one point, for example, so maybe there is still a car guy hiding in there. Auction house RM Sotheby's recently set a record for collector car auctions in Monterey, with more money changing hands that weekend than ever had in history. The wealthy car collectors are still flush with cash and willing to spend, it seems. The sale was led by the controversial $40 million Ferrari Luce charity auction, a rare $34.655 million McLaren F1 GTR sale, and an $18.7 million 1963 Corvette Grand Sport. In total the auction pushed 199 lots across the dais and nearly half of them were million-plus sales. What was that record breaking number? $380 million, meaning Musk could have used his political contribution slush fund to buy every single one of them and still have money left over for transportation, taxes, and registration.

If Musk really wants to be as popular as it seems he is desperate to be, he could have spent the summer driving around in his new Aston Martin Valkyrie Spider, Talbot-Lago T26 Record Cabriolet, Mercer Raceabout, or Lamborghini Miura P400. The point is, he could have bought whatever he wanted, but instead of something cool or useful, what he wanted was Ken Paxton.

What if he wanted to own the most expensive collector cars of all time? For just the money he spent in Texas he could easily have bought the one-of-two Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR "Uhlenhaut Coupe" which sold in 2022 for $142,000,000. In fact, for his 2026 political campaign contributions, Musk could have also purchased the Mercedes-Benz W 196 R Stromlinienwagen ($52,960,000), a Ferrari 330 LM/250 GTO ($51,705,000), another 250 GTO ($48,405,000), a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe ($42,905,000), the aforementioned Ferrari Luce, and yet two more Ferrari 250 GTOs ($38,500,000 and $38,115,000 respectively). That's the top eight most expensive cars ever sold in history. Or, you know, one feckless midterm election media buy blitz. Which would you rather have?

Let's say Elon woke up one day and felt like he wanted to do something magnanimous in an effort to repair his reputation with the American people. What could he have done with his $474,000,000 political contributions that would have instead helped the average American feel better about their country and place in it? Auto loan debt is pretty bad right now, reaching some $1.7 trillion. Obviously he couldn't clear the table on every car loan, and it would be absurd to expect him to. That said, Texas has been hit harder by auto loan debt than any other state with around 10% of borrowers in the state more than 30 days behind on their payments. How much goodwill could he garner for himself and Tesla if he were to forgive all Tesla loans in the state? That might be a good start.

Half a billion dollars buys a whole lot of goodwill for a man. Maybe he could start subsidizing grocery stores in poor Texas neighborhoods. Or pushing to fund the state's unreliable and undermaintained power grid. He could set up a fund to install EV chargers in apartment complexes or on the street, further growing Tesla's potential customer base in the state. Man, there are just so many better uses of that money than attack ads claiming James Talarico isn't manly enough to represent Texas.

My biggest takeaway from this election cycle is that America's wealthiest donor is spending his tremendous wealth trying to buy politicians. Thankfully, this time anyway, it seems that the voters have rebuked that effort. It certainly should be one of the priorities of this new crop of elected representatives to remove the ability for one man to wield this much potential political power, regardless of whether it was successful or not. It seems Americans are desperate for some kind of financial relief, whether that's reducing gas prices by ending the war in Iran, combating inflation, or making healthcare affordable, rather than fighting ridiculous culture wars. While those should be major priorities for the Democrats, campaign finance reform should probably be on the docket somewhere.

Elon seems to have made himself incredibly unpopular across the last half decade simply by aligning himself with MAGA Republicans. He's going to have a long uphill battle to revamp his image. Maybe he should just disappear from public life for a decade or so. Or buy a few hundred vintage collector cars at auction and simply give them to random American car enthusiasts. Either way, he should probably stop tweeting.

#5817. Are We Overlooking Chronic Neuropathic Pain After ICU Survival?

— Neuromodulation may offer a future treatment pathway, but better diagnosis must come first

Modern critical care has transformed survival after sepsis, respiratory failure, multi-organ dysfunction, and other life-threatening conditions. Yet, surviving an intensive care unit (ICU) admission does not necessarily mean returning to normal life.

For many patients, discharge marks the beginning of another difficult journey involving weakness, impaired mobility, sleep disturbances, cognitive difficulties, psychological distress, and persistent pain.

While post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) has received increasing attention, one potentially disabling complication deserves greater recognition: chronic neuropathic pain following critical illness.

In our recently published narrative review, "Neuromodulation for Refractory Neuropathic Pain Following Critical Illness: A Narrative Review and Phenotype-Based Clinical Framework," we examined the neurological consequences of critical illness and explored whether established neuromodulation technologies might eventually provide additional treatment options for carefully selected patients.

Our central message is straightforward: We need to identify neuropathic pain earlier, understand its underlying mechanisms, and investigate treatment strategies beyond conventional pharmacotherapy when symptoms remain disabling.

The Hidden Burden of Pain After Critical Illness

Persistent pain is an important but frequently underappreciated challenge among ICU survivors.

A systematic review reported persistent pain frequencies ranging from 28% to 77%, reflecting substantial differences in patient populations, definitions, and follow-up periods. A more recent 2026 meta-analysis estimated chronic pain incidence at approximately 47% at 3 months, 29% at 6 months, and 31% at 12 months.

These findings highlight the magnitude of the problem, but an important distinction must be made: Not all chronic pain following critical illness is neuropathic.

Patients may experience musculoskeletal pain from prolonged immobilization, muscle injury, surgical procedures, or deconditioning. Others develop peripheral nerve injuries, critical illness polyneuropathy, or potentially small-fiber pathology.

In a prospective multicenter cohort of 814 patients, nearly 48% reported significant persistent pain 3 months after ICU admission. Among those experiencing pain, approximately 9% screened positive for neuropathic pain symptoms.

These observations suggest that neuropathic pain represents a clinically meaningful subgroup requiring more specific evaluation, rather than a diagnosis that should be assigned to every patient with post-ICU pain.

Why Traditional Treatment May Not Be Enough

Critical illness polyneuropathy can involve diffuse axonal injury affecting motor and sensory nerves. Patients may experience weakness, sensory loss, burning discomfort, or other neuropathic symptoms.

However, critical illness myopathy primarily affects muscle, and weakness alone should never be interpreted as evidence of neuropathic pain. This distinction is important because treatment should be directed toward the actual source of disability.

Rehabilitation, physical therapy, psychological support, sleep optimization, and individualized medication management remain essential components of recovery.

Gabapentinoids, certain antidepressants, and topical treatments may be appropriate for selected neuropathic pain presentations. Yet, these medications can be difficult to tolerate in patients recovering from critical illness, particularly when renal dysfunction, cognitive impairment, dizziness, sedation, or respiratory vulnerability are present.

Escalating medication treatment is not always the best solution.

For patients whose persistent neuropathic pain prevents meaningful participation in rehabilitation despite appropriate conventional care, we should be asking whether additional targeted therapies deserve investigation.

Could Neuromodulation Help Selected ICU Survivors?

Neuromodulation has become an established treatment strategy for several refractory neuropathic pain conditions. Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS), dorsal root ganglion stimulation (DRGS), and spinal cord stimulation (SCS) act at different anatomical targets and have distinct evidence bases.

Our review proposes a phenotype-based framework for studying these approaches after critical illness.

PNS may be particularly relevant to focal neuropathic pain caused by positioning-related nerve injury, compression neuropathy, or other localized peripheral nerve damage. When symptoms correspond to an identifiable nerve distribution, targeted stimulation may offer a plausible research strategy.

DRGS may be relevant to selected regional neuropathic pain presentations, particularly when patients meet established diagnostic criteria for conditions such as complex regional pain syndrome or causalgia.

SCS may warrant investigation in selected patients with bilateral or multisegmental peripheral neuropathic pain, provided that the neurological diagnosis and treatment target are clearly established.

Existing clinical trials provide reasons for scientific interest.

For example, the ACCURATE trial demonstrated higher 3-month treatment success with DRGS than conventional SCS among patients with lower-extremity complex regional pain syndrome or causalgia. Similarly, the SENZA-PDN trial demonstrated substantial pain relief with 10-kHz SCS in patients with refractory painful diabetic neuropathy.

However, these findings cannot simply be transferred to patients recovering from critical illness. There is currently insufficient direct clinical evidence to establish the efficacy of PNS, DRGS, or SCS specifically for post-critical-illness neuropathic pain.

That limitation is essential. Our proposed framework is intended to guide clinical investigation, not justify routine device implantation for an unvalidated indication.

We Need a Better Bridge Between the ICU and Pain Medicine

One of the most important opportunities may lie not in new technology, but in improving coordination across specialties.

Patients frequently transition from intensive care to rehabilitation facilities, primary care, and outpatient specialty services. During these transitions, neurological symptoms and pain characteristics may not receive consistent follow-up.

A more coordinated pathway could begin with documenting neurological deficits, pain patterns, and relevant procedural or positioning exposures before ICU discharge. Subsequent assessments should distinguish persistent weakness from neuropathic pain, evaluate functional limitations, and identify patients requiring neurological investigation.

For patients with ongoing disabling symptoms, collaboration among critical care physicians, neurologists, rehabilitation specialists, primary care clinicians, and pain medicine specialists may improve diagnostic clarity and treatment planning.

Early referral to pain medicine does not mean early implantation.

Medical stabilization, adequate diagnostic evaluation, rehabilitation, psychological support, and procedural safety assessment must remain priorities.

If neuromodulation is eventually studied in this population, traditional pain intensity measurements alone will not be sufficient.

The outcomes that matter to ICU survivors often extend beyond numerical pain scores.

Can the patient walk farther? Participate more effectively in physical therapy? Sleep better? Reduce medication-related adverse effects? Resume meaningful daily activities?

These functional outcomes should be central to future investigations.

Prospective studies must also distinguish improvements in pain from neurological recovery. Reducing neuropathic pain does not necessarily reverse axonal injury, restore muscle strength, or accelerate nerve regeneration.

Long-term safety is equally important. Patients recovering from critical illness may have residual organ dysfunction, anticoagulation requirements, nutritional deficiencies, impaired wound healing, or other factors that influence procedural risk. A treatment that reduces pain but introduces disproportionate complications or care burdens may offer limited overall benefit.

The next step should not be widespread adoption of neuromodulation for post-ICU neuropathy. It should be carefully designed clinical research. As critical care continues to improve survival, our definition of successful treatment must evolve. Survival should be the beginning of recovery, not the endpoint of care.

#5816. Hyundai Motor Group Outlines Future Mobility Technology Roadmap at FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026

HWASEONG, Korea — Hyundai Motor Group (the Group) is co-hosting the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026 with the International Federation of Automotive Engineering Societies (FISITA). The two-day summit is taking place Nov. 4–5 at Rolling Hills Hotel in Hwaseong, Korea.

Founded in 1948, FISITA is a global organization that brings together automotive engineering societies and industry experts to promote knowledge exchange and technological innovation in automotive engineering. It holds the World Mobility Summit every two years, bringing together executives and technology leaders from global mobility companies to discuss industry challenges and future technology directions, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and vehicle electrification.

This year’s summit is the first to be held in Korea. Chang Hwan Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Electrification Energy Solutions Tech Unit at Hyundai Motor Group, is the first Korean to serve as FISITA President.

“Hyundai Motor Group will continue to strengthen its competitiveness in key future mobility technologies and continue to participate in technology exchange and collaboration across the global automotive industry to contribute to the development of the future mobility sector.” –Chang Hwan Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Electrification Energy Solutions Tech Unit at Hyundai Motor Group

On the first day, Manfred Harrer, President and Head of R&D Division at Hyundai Motor Group, delivered a keynote address introducing the Group’s electrification strategy. It encompasses battery electric vehicles (BEVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs). Harrer described the Group’s technology development roadmap for responding flexibly to market changes and customer needs.

Harrer also emphasized strengthening future vehicle development capabilities by combining engineering technology with AI-based digital capabilities and connecting the strengths of different technologies to pursue a sustainable mobility future.

In his opening remarks, Kim said that the automotive industry is undergoing an unprecedented technological transition. He emphasized that diverse technology approaches and stronger global collaboration are important to the advancement of future mobility.

Under the theme “Embracing the Complexities of Mobility,” the summit is addressing key technologies and challenges facing the automotive industry, including software-defined vehicles (SDVs), AI, autonomous driving, batteries and energy infrastructure.

Executives and technology leaders from across the global automotive industry are in attendance, sharing perspectives on key technology challenges and future development directions for the mobility industry.

Keynotes and panel discussions are examining major changes in the automotive industry, including advances in AI and software, the evolution of autonomous driving technology and the diversification of electrification technologies. Participants are also discussing technology directions and ways for the industry to collaborate in response to these shifts.

Major automakers are presenting vehicle and technology exhibits during the summit. The Group is displaying the Genesis GV90 and Hyundai TUCSON, along with a battery pack, hydrogen tank and robotics platform.

#5815. The Most Expensive Ford Fathom Will Still Cost Under $40,000

Good morning! It's Thursday, November 5, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, we get a better understanding of how much the upcoming Ford Fathom EV will cost, Canada is refusing to back down on its trade dispute with the U.S., Toyota is posting monster numbers and Stellantis is keeping Fiat 500 production paused for another week.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

We've known the Ford Fathom's $29,945 starting price for some time now, but we're finally getting an idea of where the mid-size electric pickup will top out at, and it sounds like it could be a real value proposition. Ford is still on track to launch Fathom pre-orders in the first quarter of 2027, according to Andrew Frick, Ford Blue and Model e President. When those preorders do start, they'll top out in the "high $30,000 range," and there will be a "couple different offerings within that."

Frick says the Blue Oval has seen prices for new battery-electric vehicles in the U.S. rise by about 10% in the past couple of years, and that has pushed many new EVs outside of the "affordable" price point for a lot of shoppers. From the Detroit Free Press:

"It's not just the EV market, it's actually opening us op to a massive total addressable market," Frick said. "If you know that nearly 50% of the U.S. new vehicle industry transacts under $40,000, not only do we expect Fathom... to attract new and used EV buyers, but also (gasoline) and hybrid customers, especially because we're going to ahve much lower operating costs than even a mainstream hybrid vehicle."

He declined to add further details at the moment other than to say Ford would add an affordable advanced electrical architecture and offer a digital camera dashboard.

[Ford CEO Jim] Farley then said, "I won't go into all the detials Andrew said, but the digital suite, including the embedded Apple Maps, is really a game changer.... let alone at this price. For me personally, that is going to be the most exciting upset opportunity. It's really the long-term subscription and digital experieence for the customer."

Of course, there are now two things Ford must prove: 1) It can actually build the Fathom on time without having it recalled a million times a week. So far this year it has issued 84 separate recalls — 43 more than second-place Stellantis. 2) It can actually see the Fathom for the prices it has mentioned for at least some amount of time. As we all remember, the Maverick once started under $20,000. Now, a base 2027 May will set you back $29,990, including destination.

A senior Canadian cabinet minister said the results of Tuesday's midterm elections weren't going to change Ottawa's stance toward trade talks with the U.S., adding that he would soon be speaking with his American counterparts. The rising costs of goods brought on by President Trump's trade wars with various countries played a huge role in the thorough drubbing Republicans took earlier this week. From Reuters:

Dominic LeBlanc, the ​minister in charge of US trade ties, ​said "to a certain extent last night's results are interesting, but ‌they ⁠will not have any significant impact in terms of our government's focus and work."

LeBlanc told reporters that he planned to speak ​to US ​Commerce Secretary ⁠Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer over the next few ​days.

Trump said on Tuesday the ​United ⁠States was close to making a trade deal with Canada, but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said ⁠work ​remained to be done ​and that Washington had dropped some demands.

It'll be interesting to see if the results of the election have changed Trump's tune on trade with Canada or if he'll now double down. After all, he's got literally nothing to lose at this point, so he could harden his position, taking us all down with him in the process. That's a fun thought, isn't it?

Toyota might have just posted its third-straight month of sales declines, but it's still raising its annual earnings forecast thanks to a weaker yen and cost cuts that boosted quarterly operating profits. CFO Yoichi Miyazaki gave more encouraging news — for shareholders, at least — saying there was further room for cost reduction, as well.

All of this is to say that operating profits climbed 34% to about $7.1 billion, and revenue was up 8.6% to about $85 billion. This good news comes despite everything going on in the Middle East right now. Toyota worked hard to mitigate those effects and others, even here in the U.S. From The Wall Street Journal:

The Japanese automaker has taken measures to mitigate the impact of disruptions caused by the Iran war, such as establishing alternative routes to shorten the time it takes to deliver vehicles to customers in the Middle East.

The carmaker has also implemented steps to expand production capacity in the U.S., after it announced a plan last November to invest up to $10 billion in the country over the next five years.

Toyota in July said it would spend $3.6 billion to bring production of its top-selling midsize pickup, the Tacoma, back to the U.S. by 2030. The company plans to build a second assembly line for the Tacoma at its San Antonio plant. Toyota currently builds the Tacoma in Mexico.

The Japanese carmaker, like many of its rivals, has been hit by the Trump administration's tariffs. Making more vehicles in the U.S. will help Toyota, the world's top-selling automaker, defray a hefty tariff bill in its largest market.

Because of the weaker yen, shipments have become more competitive abroad, according to WSJ. It also has the effect of boosting the value of profits earned overseas in yen terms. The currency has depreciated 28% against the dollar over the past five years, and it's not like the dollar is doing that hot itself.

Fiat's production is a mess right now. Its owner, Stellantis, is extending the current stoppage at its 500 plant in Turin, Italy, for the whole of next week because of a semiconductor chip shortage, according to both the automaker and the FIOM trade union. If it can't finish the engine control unit, it can't finish the car. It's more bad news for a company just looking to make money where it can at this point. From Reuters:

The November 9-13 ​extension marks the fourth consecutive week ⁠of no production at the historic ​Mirafiori plant.

Union officials have pointed at weak demand for the Fiat 500 city car as ​the continuing ​reason ⁠for the stoppage.

Gianni Mannori of the FIOM metalworkers' union said ​that blaming the shortage of ​components ⁠was "an alibi."

Last week Stellantis said the shortage in engine control units was causing "significant" ⁠disruption ​to the Italian production ​of the Fiat 500 and Fiat Pandina models.

The first two weeks of the shutdown apparently were not caused by this chip shortage. Instead, Stellantis blamed weak demand. It's certainly curious timing as to why this chip shortage would pop up all of a sudden. How convenient.

As we all know, Richard Nixon had a very cool, very chill and very low-key presidential tenure after his election. It was barely noteworthy, when you think about it. Obviously, I'm joking, but what's sort of hard to wrap your head around is the idea that what he did probably would only be a blip — a week-long news story at most — in today's day and age. #5814. You Need A New Car? Go Electric! It’s Superior Technology! Part 1

Your car is getting “long in tooth,” or maybe your daughter is going away to college and you are giving her your car. Whatever the reason, you are looking for another car. It could be new, it could be used: don’t even look at gas cars, electric cars are superior technology!

The wheels on every railroad locomotive in the world are driven by electric motors. All the busiest rail routes in Europe and China are pure electric, including high-speed rail. 98% of new cars in Norway are electric, over 80% of new cars in Denmark are electric. In China, the country with the largest sales of new cars in the world, the percentage of new electric cars in September 2026 was 67%. 82% of the operating bus fleet in China is electric. Even ships and airplanes are going electric. The data is unequivocal: electric propulsion is superior to internal combustion propulsion. Only the huge political contributions to Trump by the fossil fuel industry and his resulting anti-EV policies have slowed down adoption in this country.

In places we’ve been like California; Portland, Oregon; and northern Utah, you are seeing a lot of Teslas, so you know that electric cars are working for a lot of people these days. It’s time for you to do some research on electric cars.

You do pay a premium for new electric cars, because the batteries are still quite expensive. If price is the driving factor for you, buy a used electric car. Hardly any used EVs are high mileage, and EV batteries still have plenty of life even after they go off warranty at 8 years and 120,000 miles. There are thousands of lightly used EVs sitting at used car lots at reasonable prices all over the country these days. Some used car dealers will give you an estimate of the battery life. If not, get a friend who is an experienced EV driver to help you evaluate the battery life of the EV you are considering.

If you just do local driving or have two cars and have a garage or off-street parking, an EV is a no brainer. EVs are hands-down more convenient than gas cars for local driving. Your EV will have plenty of range for local driving, it will get a complete charge overnight in your home garage refueling station and it will never need an oil change.

EVs are as quiet as mice, as smooth as kittens, and as quick as jackrabbits. They have simple electric motors, not complex internal combustion engines. They have simple one-speed transmissions, not complex 7-speed automatic transmissions. They don’t have exhaust systems with mufflers that will rust and need replacement. They don’t have emission control systems with limited life. They don’t have complex cooling systems with big radiators. You seldom use your brakes with an EV, so your brakes may last the life of the car. They don’t have a big lead-acid battery for starting, with a maximum life of 5 years. New EVs have only a small lithium-ion battery, which lasts 10+ years. Bottom line: Routine maintenance for EVs is almost nil. I think the only real maintenance item on a Tesla over the first 3 years is the cabin air filter. You can expect an EV to go 500,000 miles without major repair or replacement in most cases.

Perhaps you can stomach buying a car from Tesla whose CEO has become one of the most despicable persons on the planet lately. (Example: Musk recently suspended access to his Starlink communications system to the Ukrainians who are valiantly defending their country from the Russian aggressors.) However, Tesla has sold almost 10 million automobiles worldwide that don’t emit CO2 and particulate pollution while operating. Tesla also has by far the most ubiquitous charging system, which allows cross-country driving on major US roads with little planning. Consider buying a Tesla.

So, what about cross-country trips? Everyone knows that long-distance trips in an electric car are inconvenient or even impossible, because there aren’t enough charging stations and it takes an hour if you can find one. Wrong: Every 100 miles along all the major Interstate highways, Tesla has built Superchargers with 8 to 32 and a few with over 100 charging stalls. By the time you have gone to the bathroom, walked the dog, and chatted with a fellow EV owner for a few minutes, you probably have more than enough charge to continue your journey. Usually, charging takes about 20 minutes. If you need a longer charge, you may need to watch a bit of Octopus Teacher or Back to the Future II on the big screen in the car for another 10 minutes.

News flash! Since February 28, 2023, most Tesla Superchargers (now North American Charging Standard/NACS chargers) are usable by all EV brands. Unfortunately, older Tesla Superchargers can’t be used by other brands, so I would still advise buying a Tesla if you want carefree cross-country driving. CCS chargers which are native to most other brands have sprung up by the thousands in the US, which together with the newer Tesla Superchargers make it possible to travel cross-country with non-Teslas on many routes with some planning. Also, Teslas can use non-Tesla chargers. Non-Tesla chargers often come with Tesla cables now, so Tesla owners don’t even need an adapter in most cases. However, even Teslas require careful planning if you are driving far from major highways.

My wife and I have done cross-country trips from Utah to Wisconsin for 7 years, on to North Carolina (once), and back to Utah. We have also traveled from Utah to Southern California at the same 500 miles per day rate that we used to do with our gas cars … and with no worries, mate.

I’m going to try to pass on some things I’ve learned from driving five different electric vehicles over 12 years and some 200,000 miles. See part two, coming soon.

This will get you a total of 3 months free Full Self Driving. It will be $99/month after that. For a Cybertruck, you will get $1000 off your purchase price. #5813. These Are The Recessionmobiles You Want Automakers To Build

Folks, it sure feels like we're trapped in the belly of a terrible machine and the machine is bleeding to death. The AI bubble threatens to pop and take the global economy with it, war with Iran is unending, we've heard it all before — the old world dying, the new one struggling to be born, yadda yadda. But even in the worst of times, we've all got to go to work and buy our groceries and take the kids to school, so we need cars that can ferry us through the time of monsters.

That's why, earlier this week, I asked you all what recessionmobiles automakers should build to get us through the next once-in-a-lifetime global financial crisis. Your answers took inspiration from all sorts of sections of the automotive world, from the oil embargo of the '70s to the very modern segment of electrically aided micro mobility. Let's dive in and see what you suggested.

Midsize sedans that start in the low $20s and end around $30 fully loaded. In a lot of trim levels, with manual transmissions and optional "big" engines that can be paired with those manuals as well. Wagon versions, coupe versions, AWD for those who want to pay an extra $1k. I miss the golden era of the family sedan from '00-'10.

We're already seeing it; e-bikes and e-scooters. Once we're all unemployed, and fuel goes to $8/gallon, it will be the only way we can afford to get around.

A recession coinciding with high fuel prices, or a possible physical shortage of fuel? The smallest and most efficient vehicles possible.

It's say just take the physically smaller half of every manufacturer's current lineup and add an actual base model trim that does away with the infotainment system, every ADAS feature, and leather/fake-leather seats, etc. Probably would've trim off much from the MSRP, but at least then there might be some new cars I'd actually consider buying.

"Automakers should sell me a Slate, but for more money" is certainly a unique take.

Chevy: Waving their hands around pointing at the Bolt which starts at 28k before incentives and seats four comfortably, with hatchback versatility and lifestyle-suggestive crossover styling, impervious to oil price swings caused by various international conflicts

I think that the rest of the world should be building cheap EVs, saving a ton of money on fuel, and being extremely demonstrative about it.

Every domestic manufacturer should offer basic subcompact 2-door and compact 4-door cars with a non-turbo 3 or 4 cylinder manual transmissions and a compact regular-cab 3 or 4-cylinder pickup truck and price them at $15,000 or below.

Imagine the possibilities if there was that much competition in the compact car and truck market. People say small cars and trucks don't sell in America, but they will if they're priced correctly.

2 words, Light and Cheap. Make something that doesn't weigh 2 tons to start. Bring back 4 cylinder non turbo cars that don't need 300+hp just to get up to highway speed. As others have said, the Maverick and Slate have shown there's a market for basic transportation. We need a modern Model T, not another Expedition.

Budget sub-brands. GM had Saturn, and Toyota had Scion. Toyota could take advantage of economies of scale to resurrect Scion as a budget-friendly, hybrid only brand. Use the Prius and Camry platforms and put quirky, boxy bodies on them for maximum utility.

The base price for a 2027 Honda Fit in Japan is ¥1,806,200 = $11,394.47 USD.

The AWD version starts at ¥2,026,200 = $12,777.67 USD.

#5812. Choosing the Initial Treatment Approach in HER2-Positive Breast Cancer

— "Beyond Diagnosis" continues with Megan Kruse on the myriad of factors that go into that decision

Developed in partnership with the Our Partner

In "Beyond Diagnosis: Early HER2-Positive Breast Cancer," Cleveland Clinic breast oncologist Megan Kruse, MD, and host John Mangels discuss how clinicians can navigate increasingly complex treatment decisions while helping patients understand their diagnosis and care.

Each installment of this series explores key aspects of early HER2-positive breast cancer care, including interpreting pathology, navigating evolving therapies, individualizing treatment, and supporting patients through shared decision-making.

In this second episode, Kruse discusses choosing between upfront surgery and neoadjuvant therapy, balancing treatment efficacy with toxicity, and tailoring treatment decisions to patients' preferences and individual circumstances.

The following is a transcript of their remarks:

Mangels: Welcome to "Beyond Diagnosis," where we talk with doctors about treatment decisions and communicating with patients. I'm your host, John Mangels. HER2-positive breast cancer is a particularly aggressive disease. Targeted therapies are improving patient treatment options, but those advances have also made care more complex.

Today, we'll explore how breast oncologists make clinical decisions, adapt treatment as new information emerges, and help patients understand their choices. Our guest is Dr. Megan Kruse. Dr. Kruse is director of breast medical oncology and co-leader of the breast cancer program at Cleveland Clinic. Dr. Kruse, thanks so much for being here.

Kruse: Thanks for having me. I'm excited about this conversation today.

Mangels: In early-stage disease, a major choice is whether treatment should begin with surgery or systemic therapy. For a patient with newly diagnosed nonmetastatic HER2-positive cancer, what features would make you lean towards surgery?

Kruse: Yeah, this is also a big topic of conversation when we first meet a patient, because I think without the HER2 knowledge, many of them come in assuming they're just going to go to surgery first because that's what happens for the vast majority of patients with breast cancer, early-stage breast cancer. So I try to explain to them that when HER2 is positive, it gives us the opportunity to give treatments before surgery to help understand how effective those treatments are.

So usually in our guidelines, we use about a 2-cm tumor as a cutoff for how large a cancer in the breast has to be to consider that preoperative chemotherapy. And any lymph node positivity generally also moves a patient into that group where we would use systemic therapy before surgery or neoadjuvant therapy, whereas the smaller tumors and negative lymph nodes, typically we would think about going to surgery first. And the reason for that really is that the intensity of the systemic therapy that we give is vastly different if you do it before surgery versus after surgery.

Mangels: What about if there is a bit of a gray area in terms of which way to go?

Kruse: Yeah, so those are our T1cN0 patients more commonly. These are tumors that are bigger than a centimeter, but less than 2 cm and node negative clinically. Those are our most challenging situations because we want to be able to personalize and adapt the systemic therapy as much as possible. And the best way to do that is to give neoadjuvant therapy, but you worry that you're being too heavy handed if you're giving these neoadjuvant regimens to patients with those smaller tumors.

And so many times I will lay that out with a patient and say, "Hey, there is some gray zone here. Here's the pluses, here's the minuses. Here's what duration of treatment would look like." Some patients really can't imagine going through 4 to 6 months of treatment with a tumor still in their body. And if that's the case and we know that we're going to make their quality of life much worse by trying to do this, maybe that pushes us one way.

These are also the great cases for tumor board again, where you say, "Hey," to your breast surgeon, "How easy do you think the surgery's going to be in the current state? Do you need me to try to shrink this tumor? Does that lymph node really look negative?" So in the gray zone cases, again, you're putting the puzzle pieces together to figure out what's the best way forward. And at the end of the day, sometimes you just have to say, "This is what my gut tells me and we're going to go with it." And most patients actually really appreciate that and they'll say, "Whatever you think is best, we should just do it."

Mangels: When neoadjuvant therapy is indicated, you as a clinician have multiple anti-HER2 agents as options. How do you weigh things like efficacy, maturity of evidence, toxicity, and patient preferences when you're making your choice?

Kruse: Yeah. It's amazing that all of those factors are going through your head at one moment in time.

Kruse: It's quite a juggling act. I would say that I come into a patient's room trying to have thought about all of this already so that I at least have my own mature sense of what I would recommend. Sometimes I go into that room and I learn about the patient and I realize I've got to flex. This plan is not going to work.

But I think when I'm coming up with that optimal plan, the first part of that is weighing largely efficacy and toxicity. When we think about these preoperative regimens in particular, the efficacy in terms of getting rid of all the cancer that you can see at the time of surgery really is our north star -- that's that pathologic complete response data point that we see in a lot of our trials. And the reason that that's so important is that pathologic complete response is an excellent surrogate for overall cancer control, overall survival, living without breast cancer recurrence.

And so when I'm looking at trials, that pathologic complete response data point is really what I'm going for because many of these trials will not have that mature survival data quite yet. But that doesn't mean I wouldn't act on that data. I'm comfortable enough with pCR (pathologic complete response) as an endpoint that we move on that.

But every improvement we've seen in pCR tends to come with some change in the side effect profile. And so that's where you have to think about which side effects are you willing to expose a certain patient to? Can they handle those? Are there long-term effects? And this is where I might view the decisions differently in a younger patient versus an older patient. Am I going to change their day-to-day functioning based on the side effects they develop? And in some of those younger patients, are there long-term consequences that if I cure them of the breast cancer, I may have to deal with a major complication 10, 15 years down the road?

So it really is a balancing act. And especially when it comes to those really long-term complications of treatment, you have to bring those up with your patients early on so that they're fully informed and that they know because some patients wouldn't be willing to take that risk. Even if it's 20% better for their cancer, they may say, "I'm not willing to worry about my heart later on." And we adapt to that.

Mangels: I'm guessing some of your patients are like, "I just want to get this tumor out of me." How do you approach and communicate with those patients that really just want to be done with the cutting part, the tumor excision part?

Kruse: Yeah. If those patients are in the gray zone based on their clinical staging, I would say we respect that decision and we may go to surgery right away. And it may change what their postsurgical systemic therapy looks like, but we still have great options. So if that is really a priority for patients, we honor that.

If there's a patient that has a larger tumor, has positive lymph nodes where I really think that neoadjuvant therapy will be important to them, I try to be as clear as possible as to why we're recommending it. And I think patients will often not realize that as we're treating with the systemic therapy that we are expecting the tumor to shrink and potentially go away. A lot of them worry that we're just getting the treatment in because we want to clear out the blood. It's really interesting that the perceptions of what chemotherapy and HER2-targeted therapy do can be all over the place when patients first come to our office.

But as you talk through that you may see this tumor shrink in real time, you may see your breasts go back to normal if it's heavier or firmer when you start treatment. And when that does happen and patients see that working, there's nothing better. They really believe in the treatment. And so being clear about what the goals are can really help with that conversation.

Mangels: It's also a learning opportunity for you as a clinician. You're seeing how that tumor responds to treatment, which is going to inform what you do going forward.

Kruse: Yeah, that's what it's all about actually. It's like an in-real-time experiment, of course an experiment that we have really excellent reasons to do. I largely tell patients that I want to know how well this treatment works on the tumor, and the only time I'm able to do that is if we still have the tumor in the breast or in the lymph nodes where we can physically feel it or see it on imaging.

Once it's cut out, we're relying on these drugs to work, but we don't really have a direct way to measure how well they're working. And actually that really resonates with patients because a lot of them want to know, did the treatment work or not? And then the counterpoint to that is if the treatment doesn't work, as disappointed as that makes all of us, it gives us an opportunity to flex after surgery and say, OK, we can use something different and try to clean up whatever may not have been killed off by the first wave of therapy.

Mangels: At the lower-risk end in patients, for example, with small node-negative tumors, how do you decide how much chemotherapy and HER2-directed therapy is adequate?

Kruse: It's a really interesting time because we're both deescalating for these low-risk patients and escalating for the higher-risk patients all at the same time. And so we're getting newer trials for these low-risk patients on a very frequent basis actually, where we're trying to remove the chemotherapy, where we're trying to lessen the number of doses of chemotherapy we're giving if we really still believe that we have to give it.

And there also are some approaches that we're using different imaging techniques to try to get a sense of really early response and escalating treatment if we're not seeing that early sign of response and then keeping the treatment lower intensity if we are seeing signs of response.

Mangels: So is that really the deciding factor for deescalation or not?

Kruse: Yeah, for the most part. If you have a lower-risk or medium-risk patient where you're still using preoperative therapy, you may see the early response as a sort of fork in the road of how intense you are with your treatment.

For those really low-risk patients where we've decided we're going to surgery first and then we're giving all of the systemic therapy after surgery, there we have a few different trial options where we can think about which particular type of chemotherapy may we want to use. Right now the conventional is HER2-targeted therapy with about 3 months of chemotherapy and then that HER2-targeted therapy continues on for the remainder of a year.

But there are some trials where we're looking at using different types of HER2-targeted therapy for various periods of time within that year to maybe have a more tolerable experience but still be really effective against the cancer.

Mangels: Are patients surprised to learn sometimes that chemotherapy doesn't have to be a part of the treatment plan?

Kruse: Absolutely, yes. And I think that...

Mangels: Surprised in a good way, I guess.

Kruse: Surprised in a good way, yeah. And we also have to do a lot of breaking down of what do these drugs actually do? What is chemotherapy? What is targeted therapy? Because many patients will assume that anything that goes in through the IV is chemo. And of course, some of our targeted therapies go through the IV, but they're not chemo and they have very different consequences for side effects, risk, how long the infusions are. And so that's a huge part of the education that we do upfront with patients.

Mangels: Chemotherapy is a familiar term with a lot of patients. Surgery, obviously people understand that, but we're talking about things like monoclonal antibodies, TKIs [tyrosine kinase inhibitors], antibody-drug conjugates. How do you explain those concepts in a way that is meaningful to patients? And do patients want to know the details of what those are or not?

Kruse: Yes, patients definitely want to know. Some are like, "OK, just give me what you think is best." But I would say most patients are wondering what the individual components of their treatment are.

Kruse: And what they do and what that means for what they can expect, or if they run into complications, which one of these are really crucial, which ones might be able to be modified or dropped. And so I typically will start with going back to that idea of HER2 being our target and which of these drugs directly go against HER2, and then which of the drugs, like chemotherapy, might affect both HER2-positive cells and general cells of the body. And that's a pretty familiar concept, like what is more specific to the cancer and what might affect my whole body.

And then when it gets into the different types of HER2-targeted medicines, monoclonal antibodies versus TKIs, monoclonal antibodies are generally IV. TKIs are generally oral. So that's kind of a nice split to explain. I don't often get into where in the cells these drugs work.

Mangels: What the effect on the receptor is.

Kruse: Right. Right. Some patients will ask that, so I'm prepared to give that information if they want it, but most patients are satisfied by saying, "OK, this is my HER2-targeted drug."

Occasionally it comes up though where you might think about using monoclonal antibodies upfront, and then if you don't have a great response, you might bring around a TKI later. And there I do find telling patients like, "Hey, this is how it works differently. One of these drugs might be more successful getting to other parts of your body, like the brain, that others would not." And actually that does resonate with them, because then they see it as, "OK, this is a way that you're helping me take care of my whole body in different ways."

Mangels: You alluded to this earlier. How do your patients' lifestyles, support systems, socioeconomic status, how do those affect the treatment decisions that you make?

Kruse: Yeah, it's huge because the best treatment plan only works if the patient's actually able to receive it and able to receive it can be so many things. It can be getting the time off of work to be able to make it to the center, having a ride to get there, having the access to supportive medications like anti-nausea medications if copays are not too high.

So I'm very fortunate that I work within a team that has multiple different providers with different levels of expertise and we can each take our part in this. So my nurse may work on one aspect of what a patient's day-to-day life is like and filling in gaps where they may not have the support at home, but maybe we have resources. Our pharmacist helps in that way as well. And our social workers are really key team members for if we can support patients during this treatment journey with different resources.

Sometimes it's education, sometimes it's personnel support like home nursing. A lot of times it's logistics, like the rides to the center. But sometimes we really do have to adjust our plans to fit whatever a patient's individual circumstances...

Mangels: I was just going to ask you, are there cases where a patient's life situation just precludes doing what you initially thought you would be doing in terms of treatment?

Kruse: Absolutely. And in those situations, you try to be creative. You try to get them the best available medication that's going to be able to fit into that lifestyle. And again, it's different for everyone. And thankfully, as the advances in the field have happened, we have more and more options that allow us to create combinations. There's a ton of data in breast cancer where we can make sure that what we're thinking about doing in a creative way is also safe. That's a huge priority, but you do have to sometimes put your thinking cap on and say, "How might we approach this?"

And again, this is a space where I rely on colleagues, where I'll present cases at tumor board because sometimes you have your blinders on and you need that fresh perspective to say, "Have you considered doing it this way?" And that's very valuable because at the end of the day, we just want to do what's best for the patients.

Mangels: Thanks so much for your insights, Dr. Kruse. And thank you for joining us on "Beyond Diagnosis," where we explore not just what physicians know, but how to effectively and compassionately share that knowledge with patients. See you next time.

#5811. You Need A New Car? Go Electric! It’s Superior Technology. Part 2

Some reasons why you shouldn’t be worried about buying an electric vehicle.

Everyone knows that electric cars are much more inconvenient than gas cars. After all, there is a gas station on every corner and it only takes 5 minutes to fill up. Electric chargers are rare, and it takes at least an hour to charge.

Wrong: If you have access to 220 volt electricity or a L2 charger at home or work, an electric vehicle is much more convenient than a gas car for 300 miles per day of local driving.

In principal: In the evening, you drive into your garage, carport or driveway and take 10 seconds to plug in, the next morning, you have a full charge and take 10 seconds to unplug.

Compare that with a gas car. You probably have to make a couple of special trips per week to the gas station, put in your credit card, grab the smelly nozzle, put it in your car, and wait five minutes to fill. Then you return the smelly nozzle to the pump.

With the gas car, every 3,000 miles, you need to go to a Jiffy Lube and sit in their smelly waiting room for an hour while they change your oil.

With the gas car, every year, you need to go to an inspection station and wait an hour in their smelly waiting room while they do an emissions check.

These three tasks are all eliminated with an electric vehicle, which makes it much more convenient for local driving.

How do you charge at home? Most electric cars come with an EVSE (Electric Vehicle Service Equipment) cable. If not, you can buy one for ~$200. On one end of the cable is the plug that goes into your car, and on the other end is an interchangeable plug. The one that comes with most cables is a standard 110V plug, but for $40 you can buy a 220V Nema 14-50 plug. Almost all RV parks have NEMA 14–50 sockets. If you have 220V service in your garage, you can have one installed for about $200. Northern Lights Electric installed one in my garage in Three Lakes Wisconsin for $130. An electrician in Saint George, Utah, installed one in our garage there for $250. It cost about $500 to have 220V service run to my garage in Lindon, UT. I had a L2 charger installed there for another $700, which I needed for my first Nissan LEAF in 2014. The L2 charger is not necessary if you have an EVSE, you only need a NEMA 14–50 outlet.

L2 charging gives you about 28 miles of range in one hour. Most EVs these days have more than 300 miles of range — so, in principle, you will charge from dead empty to full in ~11 hours. However, I am rarely at dead empty and I normally only charge to 80%, so usually I am only charging from one to five hours. Note: If you want your battery to last as long as possible, don’t charge over 80% or let the charge go below 20%. This is easier to do if you have a bigger battery.

L1 (110V) charging only gives you about 4 miles of range per hour. In principal, if you plug in next to your shaver in the bathroom, it would take three days for a full charge. However, if you drive fewer than 100 miles/day, this works.  We have friends who would need to upgrade the electrical service to the whole house to get 220V service to the garage, and they have gotten along fine with L1 charging. This works especially well since they have a second car. They also have a clothes dryer near the garage. They are able to use its 220V service or nearby Superchargers in special cases.

What if you live in a condo or other place where you can’t install your own charger? With considerable effort, my brother was able to get 220V service for L2 charging in the garage of his condo. If you have a L2 charger at work, it solves the problem. Also, there are many Superchargers in cities, and if you live near one, you can fill up there just as you would with a gas station.

The lowest price Tesla is the Model 3 RWD with seating for five, a range of 321 miles, at a price of $37,000 (see mine in the lead photo). That is plenty of range for both local and cross-country driving. However, if you want to up the range to 363 miles, you need to get the Model 3 Premium for $47,500. For only $3,000 more, you can get the base Model Y. It costs only $40,000. (See the photos below.) With the Model Y, you get a lot more room for baggage, you ride a little higher, you get a much bigger power liftgate, and you have the option of a factory-installed receiver/tow hitch, which is the one upgrade I chose because I often carry my ebikes on a rack in back. The standard Model Y seats five, but you can get the optional YL which seats 6 in three rows of captain chairs. I upgraded from my 2019 Model 3 to a base 2026 Model Y recently. You can get the premium Model Y with better external and internal styling and 363 miles of range for the RWD Model. It also comes with numerous other features, like faster charging, better audio speakers, and a small video screen for the rear seat passengers for another $5,000, as shown below. Four-wheel drive is a $2,000 option on all models and does reduce your range a little.

Every Tesla comes equipped with smart cruise control. Unfortunately, autosteer was eliminated recently unless you pay for Full Self Driving. If there is a car in front of you, you essentially have 100% self-driving until you need to make a turn. You have full automation in a traffic jam, where the car will move forward, automatically following the car in front of you.

I’m currently driving a base 2026 Model Y with FSD V14, which now costs $99/month. I can get into my car in my garage or a big parking lot or a Supercharger and without touching anything say, Hey Grok, then verbally say: Navigate me to [nearly any business, my home, or any address I dictate to the navigation]. Then FSD will drive me automatically out of my garage or the parking lot to the location requested and park my car in a parking lot or on the street (but not yet into my garage). I sit back and “supervise,” but seldom must intervene or complain about its actions as it drives.

“Tesla has introduced a new feature called Automatic Collision Evasion, which can autonomously activate Full Self-Driving (FSD) to avoid imminent collisions, even if the driver has not engaged the FSD system. This feature aims to enhance safety by allowing the vehicle to take evasive actions during critical situations.”

Note: In my opinion, Tesla customers that don’t opt in for the $99/month FSD subscription are missing a very important, possibly live saving safety feature.

There are literally 161 different new EV models to choose from in the US today. There are also several EV models that have been discontinued that you can buy used. If you can’t stomach buying a Tesla from Elon Musk’s company, you can choose one of those.

I will present two good alternatives to buying a Tesla: The top selling EVs in the US in 2026 to date right now are as follows. You can see that the Teslas are by far the most sold, but the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and the Toyota bz are reasonable alternatives for Musk haters.

Toyota led the movement towards automobiles that are more friendly to the environment with the Prius over 20 years ago. However, they were very slow to offer a compelling pure battery electric vehicle. That has now changed, Toyota’s bz EV has received excellent reviews. I had been a big customer of Toyota gas cars until recently, so I dropped down to the nearest Toyota dealership to see the status of EVs there, as shown in the photos below. I was pleased that the dealer had four bzs in stock and I took one for a quick spin. It had the usual excellent Toyota workmanship, with spectacular acceleration like all EVs. However, the driving automation, like in the Corolla I had rented in the spring, is lame. The lane assist will only work on gentle turns.

Tesla keeps changing the program, but here’s the latest: If you are buying a new Tesla Model 3 or Y and use my link, you will get two months of free Full Self Driving (a ~$200 value) on top of the one month that comes free with every new Model Y right now. This will get you a total of 3 months free Full Self Driving. It will be $99/month after that. For a Cybertruck, you will get $1000 off your purchase price. At this moment, Tesla is offering a year of free Supercharging with the purchase of a new Model 3 Premium or Performance.

#5810. 1968 Ford Mustang For Sale Is A Clean, Green V8 Cruiser Begging To Be Driven Daily

When you hear "green 1968 Ford Mustang," you likely picture one very specific car. You know the one: a verdant, tire-killing fastback driven by mercurial automotive and Hollywood legend Steve McQueen in the 1968 film "Bullitt." Today, a first-generation Ford Mustang Fastback similar to the one from the 58-year-old action-crime thriller could demand six figures, especially in that oh-so coveted color: Highland Green. For first-gen Mustang fans who can't afford to spend fixer-upper-home money on a car, there are alternatives. Alternatives like this green 1968 Ford Mustang.

At a glance and on paper, it ticks boxes. A V8 under the hood? Of course. That classic facelifted first-generation Mustang look? Thankfully, it's intact. Mostly. See, someone thought this one was deserving of a cool restomod treatment, and it got just that. Instead of being a numbers-matching carbureted survivor, this one benefits from a myriad of modern and aftermarket updates, like electronic fuel injection, electric fans, power locks, keyless entry, and Vintage Air air-conditioning and heat. This is a daily-driver-ready take on a classic. It's up for grabs, too. As of this writing, the restomod-ed Mustang is for sale just north of Dallas. Purists need not apply.

No, it's not finished in Highland Green. Not even close, really. The 1968 Ford Mustang restomod currently for sale by PC Classic Cars in Sherman, Texas is a much lighter hue. The headlights have been replaced with an integrated LED lamp-and-signal set and the tail lights are sequential like an aftermarket set you'd find on a much newer Mustang. It also rides on a set of staggered two-tone Halibrand-style alloy wheels that complement the paintwork, wrapped up in Nitto rubber. The builder also swapped in a Mustang II front end, complete with a sway bar and tubular control arms.

Under the hood, the '68 Mustang gets a familiar engine option: a 289-cubic-inch V8. It's far from stock, though. The parts list continues with a set of aluminum AFR cylinder heads, a Holley Sniper EFI setup, a Fi-Tech electronic ignition, an aftermarket serpentine system, an aluminum radiator in place of the tired old stock unit, and dual electric fans, to name a few things. The whole thing hooks up to a four-speed automatic gearbox with overdrive. Sorry, no manual here.

There are more modern touches beyond the engine bay, including power locks with keyless entry via an aftermarket fob, a stereo system with an amplifier and subwoofers, and that Vintage Air climate control. The restomod treatment continues inside the classic Mustang's cabin. It's a full brown leather TMI interior with black accents on the folding bucket seats and dash paneling. The brown leather even extends into the trunk.

It's not perfect. A glance at the driver's side door reveals a little misalignment. The car was once red. There are blemishes here and there. In short, this is more of a driver, less of a concours condition car meant to be kept out of the rain or prolonged direct sunlight. That doesn't mean the modified pony car loses the aesthetic charm that landed the 1968 model on the list of your favorite Ford Mustangs. Well, the fastback did, at least.

So just how much does PC Classic Cars want for this one? It's currently on sale for $46,950. That's quite a bit steeper than the average $25,310 price of 1968 Ford Mustang coupé sales over the last year. Then again, not every '68 Mustang on the market has had this much work done.

Get this: Its clock shows just 119 miles. Though, as you might expect, that's not exactly accurate. It's likely that this build's underpinnings have a much higher mileage. Frankly, a 1968 Ford Mustang with a 289-cubic-inch V8 and an true odometer reading anywhere near 119 would demand a much, much higher price. Still, with the modern tweaks already on this 58-year-old 'Stang, it seriously needs a driver to take it on as a daily and run that odometer up. After all, what would McQueen do? He'd almost certainly drive it — and so should the next owner.
